newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro shares up ahead of US data,dollar gains.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro shares up ahead of US data,dollar gains.

text.p: European stock markets opened trading in more confident mood on Friday, regaining some lost ground before key U.S. jobs data that could clarify the outlook for future interest rate moves.

On the foreign exchange market, the dollar also rose after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said currencies should not be used as trade policy weapons -- although he urged Japan to stop its trade surplus ballooning further.
"The comments (by Rubin) suggest the dollar is still in an uptrend and dollar/yen should go higher," said Stuart Frost, currency analyst at NatWest Markets.

Dealers said any exceptional strength in U.S. March jobs and earnings figures at 1330 GMT would suggest that the Federal Reserve could raise rates again next month -- following last week's quarter-point rise -- to head off inflationary pressures in the world's biggest economy.
This would jolt Wall Street again and take other world markets down in its wake.
"It could be a killer if it goes the wrong way," commented Jim Benning, a trader at BT Brokerage in New York, looking ahead to the jobs data.
Economists surveyed by Reuters expected U.S. non-farm payrolls to show a rise of 196,000 for March and average earnings to be up 0.4 percent.
The London stock market, Europe's busiest, rose in line with bonds on selective early buying after recent falls, boosted by Wall Street's recovery from its lows.
"It was encouraging that the wheels didn't come off on Wall Street. There was selling but no blind panic," a dealer said. "But now we will all be waiting for the U.S. numbers."

U.S. blue-chip stocks dropped on Thursday for the fourth time in five sessions but closed well above their lows. The Dow fought back from a 95-point decline to end almost 40 points off at 6,477.35, while the technology-rich Nasdaq index rose around one percent.

London dealers said trade was likely to stay thin and nervous before the U.S. data, with one commenting: "Nobody wants to put their neck on the block before these numbers. There's no point taking the risk."
Britain's election campaign, just under four weeks from the May 1 polls, was of less concern.
In Frankfurt, buying interest focused on export-driven chemical and car industries lifted German shares but dealers were wary about prospects after sharp recent losses.
"Monday is the earliest we will really be able to tell if we have found a real floor," said one Frankfurt dealer.
French stocks also rebounded after three days of decline but trading was expected to remain cautious before the U.S. figures.
But Thomson-CSF shares fell 2.54 percent to 188.10 francs. The Figaro newspaper said the government would not accept Britain's GEC as a candidate to take it over.
Elsewhere, the Swiss, Dutch and Italian bourses were among those markets in the plus column.

The dollar rose after Rubin, who had recently spooked it by warning Japan not to let its huge trade surplus swell again, repeated similar comments in Tokyo -- but rejected the notion that a stronger yen was the best way to act.
"We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else," he told reporters.
Analysts said strong U.S. jobs and earnings data later in the day could boost the dollar but countering this could be concern over the likelihood of further falls in U.S. asset markets.
Meanwhile, for those with a more long-range focus, European Union finance ministers arrive in the Netherlands for an informal meeting until Sunday to discuss economic and monetary union.
CURRENCIES AT 0930 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.6758 marks and 123.98 yen, up from 1.6681 and 122.59 in late European trade on Thursday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 0930 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 24.4 points or 0.58 percent at 4,239.0.
PARIS - The CAC-40 gained 12.76 points or 0.51 percent to 2,527.28.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was up 19.31 points or 0.60 percent at 3,234.55.
PRECIOUS METALS at 0930 GMT

Gold was quoted around $347.55 an ounce, down from the previous London close of $348.65. Silver slipped to $4.74 from $4.83 and dealers expected further selling, particularly from one large U.S. fund.
